transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Lena from Redwood. We got Miguel on the line from SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Aisha Rahman: Doing well, thanks. Quick heads up we're on a tight timeline so want to focus on sizing and burst behavior.
[00:12] Miguel Ortiz: Great, thanks Aisha. Agenda for today: go over the benchmark numbers from last week, talk autoscale policies and burst, and confirm next steps.
[00:20] Tom Becker: Sounds good.
[00:25] Maya Li: Hi all. I've got the raw logs ready if you need them.
[00:30] Lena Park: Perfect. Miguel, do you want to kick off with the numbers?
[00:33] Miguel Ortiz: Sure. So we ran two workloads last Tuesday: a 2k-token typical inference and a 10k long context test. For the 2k, steady-state throughput on the 4xA40 dedicated pool was about 220 qps, 95th latency ~180ms, 99th ~320ms. For 10k, throughput dropped as expected to ~40 qps, 95th latency at 1.8s, 99th at 3.2s. Note: these have some transcription / logging noise so numbers are +/-10%.
[01:10] Tom Becker: Wait, 220 qps on 2k tokens seems optimistic. Did you measure tail with KV cache primed?
[01:15] Miguel Ortiz: Yes, that measurement had KV cache warm for the top 30% prefixes. Cold-starts for new sessions were closer to 140 qps and tail latencies bumped 40-60% on 99th. We also tested batching windows: 5ms batching gave best cost/latency tradeoff for that workload.
[01:38] Aisha Rahman: Our main concern is the morning surge between 08:00-09:30 where qps spikes 4x baseline for ~20 mins. We need burst capacity for that, and we can't accept meaningful tail degradation.
[01:50] Miguel Ortiz: Understood. For burst planning we generally recommend a two-layer approach: reserved dedicated baseline to cover steady and sustained load, plus autoscale policy that allows fast horizontal scale to cover short bursts with a warm-up buffer. Also consider burst capacity — temporary additional nodes that can spin up faster using a pre-warmed image or a hot-pool.
[02:10] Lena Park: To be concrete, Miguel, can you say how many extra GPUs they'd need to handle a 4x spike on the 220 qps baseline?
[02:18] Miguel Ortiz: Quick math: baseline 220 qps per pool at 4xA40 config, so a 4x spike is ~880 qps. If one pool supports 220 qps steady, you'd need about 4x capacity total. But because of warm cache and batching the effective capacity during spikes can be ~1.6x per node. So we'd likely provision 2x baseline reserved and configure autoscale to scale to 4x by adding 2 additional pools — also enable burst hot-pool for instant 20-30% capacity while nodes finish joining.
[02:49] Tom Becker: How fast does autoscale react? Our SREs worry about spin-up time and throttling.
[02:55] Miguel Ortiz: Default scale policy uses agent-based warm pools and typically can route warm container processes in under 30-45s. Cold node provisioning is in the 2-5 min range depending on cloud region. That's why the hot-pool is important: it keeps a small set of nodes warm for sub-minute instant bursts.
[03:16] Maya Li: Do you have cost delta estimates for keeping a hot-pool of, say, 1 GPU versus just relying on ASG style spin-ups?
[03:22] Miguel Ortiz: Rough estimate: hot-pool 1 GPU in Dedicated for a month is roughly one-tenth of a full reserve of a GPU node since it can be billed as kept-warm smaller instance — but I'll send exact numbers in the sizing sheet. The tradeoff is paying for immediate capacity vs. risk of tail latency during spin-up.
[03:36] Aisha Rahman: We also need to confirm audit logging/retention — we can't keep raw transcripts beyond 90 days and logs must be encrypted with our KMS.
[03:44] Lena Park: Absolutely, that's in scope. Miguel, is Redwood Private/VPC setup compatible with their KMS?
[03:49] Miguel Ortiz: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS / HSM. For this POC we tested with customer KEK and logs can be pushed to their cloud logging with encryption. We'll include SOC2/ISO cert references in the docs link.
[04:05] Tom Becker: Another question — model quantization. We tried int8 locally and saw some accuracy drift on the long context. Any guidance?
[04:12] Miguel Ortiz: Good point. For long context models quantization can affect logits slightly; we recommend A/B testing int8 candidate on a subset of prompts and measuring quality delta. For latency-sensitive paths, int8 gives big perf wins but preserve a fallback to fp16 variant for critical calls. We also support hybrid quant profiles so you can quantize some layers and keep others fp16.
[04:38] Maya Li: On KV cache, we saw hit rates around 62% in the logs. Is there an easy knob to improve that?
[04:45] Miguel Ortiz: Cache hit depends on session stickiness and prefix reuse. We can increase TTL for common prefixes and enable smarter prefix routing to co-locate similar traffic. Also batching policy adjustments can improve effective hit-rate since shared prefixes get batched. We'll recommend config changes in the sizing doc.
[05:05] Aisha Rahman: From procurement side, any blockers on committed Reserved capacity? We prefer a 6-month commit to start.
[05:12] Lena Park: That's totally doable; we have monthly and annual commit options. For POC we'd typically do a temporary reserved commit for the pilot period or a refundable test commit. I'll follow up with pricing options in the spreadsheet.
[05:24] Tom Becker: Back to autoscaling policies — what metrics should we use to trigger scale vs throttle? CPU/GPU utilization is noisy for inference.
[05:32] Miguel Ortiz: We recommend request-latency percentiles and queue depth as primary triggers. GPU utilization can be a secondary signal. Set scale-up when 95th latency > target or queue depth > threshold; scale-down with hysteresis windows to avoid flapping. Example: scale-up when 95th latency > 300ms for 30s, add n nodes; scale-down if 95th latency < 200ms for 5m. We'll include example policy templates.
[06:03] Maya Li: Any notes on routing policy if a region hits capacity? We need failover to another region with minimal cold-start impact.
[06:10] Miguel Ortiz: Use smart routing with regional fallback and model variant compatibility. You can route lower-tier traffic to a slightly cheaper model to preserve capacity in primary region. Cross-region failover will incur KV cache warmup; mitigations: sync hot-pool across regions or replicate KV cache for critical prefixes.
[06:29] Aisha Rahman: Let's capture a concrete pilot success criteria: keep 95th latency under 400ms for 2k requests and under 2s for 10k requests during peak bursts, with error rate <0.1% and cost not exceeding the target we'll share. If those hold for two weeks we move to Dedicated commit.
[06:46] Lena Park: Great, we'll formalize that in the next doc. Any other blockers?
[06:52] Tom Becker: One small item — network egress controls. We need to ensure outbound access is locked down for the Private setup.
[06:58] Miguel Ortiz: Private supports VPC egress controls and firewall rules. We'll add the architecture note and a sample network policy.
[07:07] Maya Li: Okay. Regarding benchmarks — are you able to simulate our morning surge pattern?
[07:12] Miguel Ortiz: Yes, we can run a synthetic load matching your histogram. We'll need the per-minute qps and a target concurrency pattern; Tom, can you drop the CSV?
[07:20] Tom Becker: I'll upload to the shared folder after the call.
[07:24] Lena Park: Perfect. We'll plan to run the surge sim in the 05-06 window next week to avoid production conflict.
[07:31] Miguel Ortiz: Quick note on cost optimization: enabling prefix caching + aggressive batching for non-interactive flows reduces token unit cost by ~25-35% in our tests. For interactive user flows where latency matters, keep batching smaller.
[07:47] Aisha Rahman: That aligns with our use cases — some batch-ish backfill analytics plus interactive triage.
[07:52] Maya Li: One more thing: the 10k test had a couple of anomalous 99th spikes around 6s. Any idea?
[07:58] Miguel Ortiz: Likely GC or the node hitting a cold swap path; we saw a misrouted request that forced a cold KV lookup. We'll correlate logs, but increasing hot-pool and improving routing should eliminate those outliers.
[08:12] Tom Becker: Ok. On documentation, can you send the compliance packet and also a short deck on dedicated sizing?
[08:18] Lena Park: Yes, will send links: sizing spreadsheet, compliance docs, and example autoscale policies.
[08:23] Aisha Rahman: Thank you. For timeline, after we get the extra benchmark results we'll reconvene and decide whether to convert the POC to a short-term reserved commit.
[08:33] Lena Park: Sounds good. Let's recap next steps. Miguel?
[08:36] Miguel Ortiz: Actions: run 10k-token benchmark with 16 concurrent streams, test surge sim next week, provide hot-pool cost estimates, and share example autoscale policy templates.
[08:46] Tom Becker: I'll share the traffic CSV and confirm the surge window.
[08:50] Maya Li: I'll validate quantization candidate and report quality delta.
[08:54] Aisha Rahman: We'll review the pricing sheet when you send it.
[08:58] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via the shared folder and set the benchmarking slot. Bye.
[09:03] Call ended
